l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: Penelope writes to Ulysses, urging him to return and lamenting that he has sent no reply. She recalls her fears during the Trojan War and rejoices that Troy has fallen and Ulysses survived, but his continued absence leaves her uncertain and distressed. Suitors from Dulichium, Samos, and Zacynthus occupy Ulysses's hall, consume his resources, and pressure Penelope to remarry. Penelope remains faithful to Ulysses while protecting Telemachus and caring for the aged Laertes.

l: Penelope, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: Penelope sends a letter to Ulysses, asking him to return because she has received no reply and does not know where he is. She describes her fears, her loneliness, the pressure from the suitors, and her continuing loyalty to him.

l: Odysseus, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: Ulysses has survived the Trojan War and the fall of Troy, but he remains absent and gives Penelope no certain information about the cause or location of his delay. He is remembered for his role in the night attack on the Thracian camp and for helping destroy Troy.

l: Troy, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: Troy has been destroyed and reduced to ashes. Its former site is now cultivated land, where crops grow among the bones of the dead and grass covers the ruined houses.

l: Telemachus, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: Telemachus has learned from Nestor about Ulysses's deeds in the Trojan War and has brought the account to Penelope. He was recently almost killed while preparing to go to Pylos against the wishes of those around him.

l: Laertes, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: Laertes is an aged and largely powerless defender of Ulysses's household. He urges Penelope to leave her widowed bed, but her fidelity and prayers temper his insistence.

l: the suitors, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: The suitors from Dulichium, Samos, and Zacynthus crowd into Ulysses's hall and act as its masters. They seek Penelope, consume Ulysses's resources, and include Pisander, Polybus, Medon, Eurymachus, Antinous, Irus, and Melanthius.

l: Trojan War, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: The Trojan War caused Penelope constant fear for Ulysses, especially whenever she heard of the deaths of Greek warriors. Ulysses took part in the killing of Rhesus and Dolon and in the night attack on the Thracian camp.

l: the burning of Troy, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: The fall of Troy brings the Greek leaders home and leads to sacrifices, offerings, and the display of Trojan spoils. Although Troy has fallen, Penelope gains little comfort because Ulysses remains away.

l: Penelope's fidelity, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: Penelope declares that she remains Ulysses's wife and will always be called Penelope, the wife of Ulysses. She refuses to leave her widowed bed despite her father's pressure and the suitors' demands.

l: Ulysses's absence, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: Ulysses's prolonged absence causes Penelope to fear every danger of land and sea and even to suspect that he may be held by another love. His absence also allows the suitors to dominate his household and endanger Telemachus.

l: the letter, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: The letter is written by Penelope and sent to Ulysses through any traveler who reaches her shores and might see him. She asks the recipient to deliver it to him because she has no reliable news of his whereabouts.

l: the suitors' threat, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
s: The suitors' presence threatens Penelope's marriage, Ulysses's household, and the household's resources. Their hostility also places Telemachus in danger, as he was nearly taken by ambush while preparing to travel to Pylos.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, II
s: Phyllis writes to Demophoon from Rhodope, complaining that he has not returned after promising to come within a stated time. She recalls how she welcomed him, aided him, gave him gifts and her virginity, and trusted his words, tears, oaths, and promises of marriage. She watches the sea for his ships, imagines excuses for his delay, and fears that he now has another wife. In despair, Phyllis threatens suicide and declares that Demophoon will be named on her tomb as the cause of her death.

Phyllis, who welcomed Demophoon to Rhodope, gave him refuge, gifts, aid, and her virginity, reproaches him for failing to return. She continues watching the sea for his ships, but in despair considers throwing herself into the waves, taking poison, using a sword, or hanging herself.

Demophoon promised Phyllis that he would return, but he remains absent and has not kept his word. He accepted her hospitality, aid, gifts, love, and trust before departing, and Phyllis says he may now have another wife.
Rhodope is the region where Phyllis received Demophoon and ruled broad realms. It is described as icy and extending toward Haemus.

Thrace is Demophoon's destination or homeland in Phyllis's account, and its people will not marry her because she is said to have preferred a foreigner to her own countrymen. Phyllis says she gave Demophoon the realms of Lycurgus in Thrace.

l: the sea, Heroides and Amores, II
s: The sea has kept Demophoon from returning, although Phyllis repeatedly watches its winds and waters for signs of his approach. She threatens to throw herself into it so that its waves may carry her body to Demophoon's shores.

l: the ships, Heroides and Amores, II
s: Demophoon's ships departed from Phyllis's harbor after she helped refit his damaged vessels and supplied him with oars. Their sails have not returned, and Phyllis repeatedly mistakes distant sails for his ships.

l: the oath, Heroides and Amores, II
s: Demophoon swore by the sea, his grandsire, Venus, Juno, the gods, and the rites of marriage that he would return and honor his promises. Phyllis asks where his oaths, pledged hand, and repeated references to the gods have gone.

Marriage was promised to Phyllis as a lasting bond and served as her assurance when she accepted Demophoon. She now regrets having added the marriage bed to her hospitality and fears that Demophoon has another wife.

l: Phyllis's death, Heroides and Amores, II
s: Phyllis says that Demophoon will be named on her tomb as the cause of her death. She declares that he will have caused it, while she herself will have supplied the hand.

Phyllis contemplates suicide because Demophoon continues to deceive and abandon her. She considers drowning, poison, a sword, and a noose, and says that she will not delay in choosing a means of death.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, III
s: Briseis writes to Achilles, pleading with him to reclaim her after Agamemnon demanded her return. She accuses Achilles of delaying her restoration and refusing the gifts offered by Agamemnon, while recalling the destruction of her home and the deaths of her family and husband. She urges Achilles to end his anger, return to battle against Hector, and allow her to accompany him. Briseis declares that without him she would rather die, but asks him to preserve the life he once gave her and order her to come with him.

Briseis writes to Achilles in grief, accusing him of failing to reclaim her and of allowing her to remain separated from him. She recalls the destruction of Lyrnesus, the deaths of her three brothers and husband, and her captivity, then begs Achilles either to take her back or to let her die. She offers to follow him as a captive or serve him humbly if he returns to Phthia.

Achilles has refused to restore Briseis and is said to oppose her return, despite the gifts and appeals brought by Phoenix, Ulysses, and Ajax. He remains withdrawn from the fighting, playing the lyre and enjoying the company of a mistress, while Hector attacks the Danaans. Briseis urges him to overcome his anger, reclaim her, and return to battle.

Agamemnon demanded Briseis and had her delivered to him. He later regretted his anger and offered Achilles gifts, Lesbian women, and one of his daughters as a bride, but Achilles still did not reclaim Briseis.

l: Trojan War, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The fighting continues while Achilles refuses to participate, and Hector is damaging the Danaan forces. Briseis urges Achilles to take up his armor and fight, saying that his anger began because of her and should end through her return.

l: Briseis's captivity, Heroides and Amores, III
s: Briseis was captured when Achilles destroyed Lyrnesus and killed her husband and three brothers. She was then taken from Achilles and delivered to Agamemnon, and she fears being left behind or given to another man. She says that her captivity was once presented to her as a gain because it brought her to Achilles.

l: Achilles' anger, Heroides and Amores, III
s: Achilles' anger began with Agamemnon's taking of Briseis and has kept him from fighting for the Danaans. Briseis asks him to conquer his anger, since Agamemnon now regrets his own wrath and Greece lies distressed before him. She wants her return to be both the cause and the end of his anger.

l: Briseis's letter, Heroides and Amores, III
s: Briseis's letter is written in Greek by her barbarian hand and is marked by tears that have blotted the writing. It complains of Achilles' delay, recalls her suffering, and repeatedly asks him to reclaim her. The letter ends by asking Achilles, whether he sails or remains, to command her to come as his captive or servant.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, IV
s: Phaedra writes to Hippolytus, confessing that Love has overcome her modesty and caused her to desire him. She presents her late and intense passion as a fate inherited from her family, citing Europa, Pasiphae, and Ariadne. Phaedra praises Hippolytus's appearance and hunting skills, urges him to abandon his exclusive devotion to Diana, and asks him to return her love. She also attacks Theseus for neglecting their marriage and wronging both her and Hippolytus, then begs Hippolytus to accept her despite their relationship as stepmother and stepson.

Phaedra confesses her love for Hippolytus and says that Love has made her write what modesty prevented her from saying. She describes herself as consumed by an unseen wound, adopts interests associated with Hippolytus's hunting life, and begs him to accept her. She invokes her family history, criticizes Theseus, and pleads with Hippolytus to soften his hard heart.

Hippolytus is addressed as the son of an Amazon and as a vigorous, stern, handsome hunter. Phaedra praises his horsemanship, spear-throwing, hunting, appearance, and masculine bearing. She urges him to give up some of his hardness and devotion to Diana and to return her love.

Theseus is absent while he remains with Pirithous, and Phaedra claims that he has preferred Pirithous to both her and Hippolytus. She accuses Theseus of killing her brother, abandoning her sister to wild beasts, killing Hippolytus's mother, refusing to marry her, and neglecting their marriage.

Love commands Phaedra to write to Hippolytus and is presented as a power that rules even the gods. Phaedra says that Love came to her late and therefore burns more fiercely, overcomes her modesty, and drives her to humble supplication.

l: Phaedra’s letter, Heroides and Amores, IV
s: Phaedra’s letter greets Hippolytus, asks him to read it, and carries her secrets across land and sea. It reveals her confession of love, praises Hippolytus, attacks Theseus, proposes that Phaedra and Hippolytus unite, and ends with tears and a plea for forgiveness.

l: Theseus and Phaedra’s marriage, Heroides and Amores, IV
s: Phaedra says that she would not break her marriage bond through wanton baseness and that her reputation has been free from reproach. She argues that Theseus neglects their marriage and urges Hippolytus to disregard the names of stepmother and stepson. She proposes that their union could remain openly disguised as a family relationship because they already share one household.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Oenone writes to Paris, recalling their former love and accusing him of abandoning her for Helen. She describes Paris’s departure by ship, his return with Helen, and the grief caused by seeing the new wife cling to him. Oenone argues that Helen’s former abduction and infidelity make her untrustworthy, while Oenone herself has remained faithful. She warns that Paris’s choice will bring war and offers her own healing knowledge, though she cannot cure her love for him.

l: Oenone, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Oenone identifies herself as a fountain nymph famous in the Phrygian forests and writes to Paris as his abandoned wife. She recalls their life together, mourns his departure and return with Helen, condemns his new marriage, and asks him to return to her.

l: Paris, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Paris was once a poor slave and shepherd who lived with Oenone, but he later became Priam’s son and left her. He sailed away, returned with Helen, and is accused by Oenone of choosing a stolen wife over his homeland and former love.

l: Helen, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Helen is described as the Greek woman whom Paris brought to Troy after leaving Oenone. Oenone calls her an adulteress who had previously been carried away by Theseus and argues that she cannot be trusted to remain faithful.

l: Paris's new wife, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Paris’s new wife arrives by ship with him and is seen clinging to him when the vessel reaches shore. Oenone presents her as a rival who has abandoned her lawful husband and whose presence will bring danger to Paris and Troy.

l: Xanthus, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Xanthus is the river beside which Oenone and Paris’s shared memory is preserved. Oenone calls on its waters to turn backward because Paris has deserted her.

l: letter, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: The letter is written by Oenone to Paris and begins by asking whether he will read it or whether his new wife forbids him. It records Oenone’s memories, grief, accusations, warnings, and continuing plea for Paris to belong to her again.

l: the ship carrying Paris, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: The ship is built from felled firs and hewn timbers, receives its waxed sails, and carries Paris away. Oenone later recognizes its sails, sees Helen aboard, and watches it reach the shore.

l: the Judgment of Paris, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: The Judgment of Paris is recalled as the day when Venus, Juno, and Minerva appeared before Paris to be judged. Oenone says that this event marked the beginning of the disastrous change in Paris’s love.

l: Paris's departure from Oenone, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Paris’s departure is associated with tears, embraces, repeated kisses, and difficulty saying farewell. Oenone watches his sails leave, follows them with her eyes, and wets the sand with her tears.

l: Paris's return with Helen, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Paris returns by ship, but he returns for another woman rather than for Oenone. Oenone recognizes Helen aboard, sees her in Paris’s embrace, tears at her face and breast, and fills Ida with lamentation.

l: Trojan War, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: The unit presents the coming conflict as a consequence of Paris’s choice of Helen. Oenone says that Helen is being demanded back by hostile arms and that her presence will carry Phrygian blood and bring war to Troy.

l: love between Oenone and Paris, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Oenone and Paris once loved one another while living among flocks, resting under trees, sharing a humble bed, and hunting together. Oenone insists that their love was joined by embraces and tears and that she still wants to remain Paris’s wife.

l: marital fidelity and chastity, Heroides and Amores, Oenone Paridi 2
s: Oenone presents herself as chaste and faithful despite Paris’s betrayal. She argues that Helen’s past abduction and rapid transition to Paris show a lack of fidelity, and she warns Paris that wounded chastity cannot be restored.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Hypsipyle writes to Jason after hearing that he has returned safely from his voyage with the Golden Fleece and has taken Medea as a wife. She recalls their marriage on Lemnos, Jason’s promises, his departure, and the birth of their twin sons. She condemns Medea’s magic and betrayal, contrasts Medea with herself, and urges Jason to return to her and the children. She ends by wishing suffering on Jason and Medea for abandoning her.

Hypsipyle writes to Jason, reproaching him for failing to send word of his return and for taking Medea as his wife. She recalls that she welcomed Jason on Lemnos, bore his twin sons, and remains his lawful wife; she also prays that Medea will suffer as she has suffered.

Jason is said to have returned safely to Thessaly after overcoming the trials of Mars’s bulls, the armed earth-born men, and the dragon guarding the Golden Fleece. He had promised Hypsipyle that he would return as her husband, but instead returned with Medea and abandoned her and their twin sons.

Medea is described as a barbarian poisoner who accompanied Jason and took the marriage-bed promised to Hypsipyle. Hypsipyle condemns her for magical practices, for betraying her father, and for having won Jason through crime and enchantment.
Lemnos is Hypsipyle’s homeland and forms part of the marriage portion she offers Jason. Hypsipyle says that she rescued her father from the massacre on Lemnos and that Lemnos still retains her.

l: the Argo, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The Argo carries Jason and his companions away from Lemnos after Jason boards it last. Hypsipyle watches the ship depart from a tower, seeing Jason’s land recede while she looks out over the sea.

l: the Golden Fleece, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Jason is reported to have taken the golden fleece from the ram of Phrixus, which had been guarded by an ever-watchful dragon. Hypsipyle questions whether Jason or Medea deserves the credit for obtaining it.

l: the twin sons of Jason and Hypsipyle, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Hypsipyle has borne Jason twin sons, whom she describes as resembling their father and as sharing his features except for his capacity for deceit. She nearly sent the children to Jason as their mother’s messengers but held back because she feared Medea.

l: the marriage between Hypsipyle and Jason, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The marriage between Hypsipyle and Jason was publicly sanctioned by Juno and Hymen, with wedding rites and a marriage torch. Hypsipyle presents it as chaste and legitimate, unlike Jason’s union with Medea, and asks to remain Jason’s wife after his return.

l: Jason's voyage to Colchis and abduction of the maiden, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Jason’s voyage takes him from Lemnos to the lands associated with the Golden Fleece, where he completes the trials involving Mars’s bulls, the earth-born warriors, and the dragon. After the voyage he returns safely to Thessaly, but he does not return to Hypsipyle as promised.

l: Medea's magic, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Medea’s magic is said to include incantations, enchanted herbs, the power to draw down the moon, stop waters, move forests and rocks, gather bones from funeral pyres, curse absent people, and pierce wax images. Hypsipyle claims that Medea used such arts to win and control Jason.

l: the pregnancy and birth of twins, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Jason knew that Hypsipyle was pregnant when he left and hoped that the child would live so that they could share parenthood. Hypsipyle later gave birth to twins with the help of Lucina and identifies them as pledges belonging to both parents.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, VII
s: Dido addresses Aeneas as he prepares to leave Carthage for Italy, accusing him of abandoning her and breaking his promises. She recalls how she received Aeneas, gave him power in Carthage, and entered into a love affair with him, but now fears that he will abandon her while she is pregnant. Dido urges him to remain, warning that the sea is dangerous and that faithlessness will bring punishment. She ultimately prepares for suicide, describing the sword in her lap and asking Anna to give her final funeral offerings.

Dido pleads with Aeneas not to leave her and recalls that she received him when he was cast ashore, gave him her kingdom, and loved him despite his faithlessness. She says she is pregnant, fears abandonment, and prepares to die by the sword.

Aeneas is determined to leave Dido and follow Italy, despite the new city, walls, power, and love available to him in Carthage. Dido portrays him as ungrateful, faithless, and repeatedly deceptive, while also urging him to survive the sea and spare Ascanius.

Carthage is described as a newly founded city with rising walls, a kingdom, peoples, and power that Aeneas is abandoning. Dido offers Carthage and its wealth as an alternative to Aeneas's pursuit of Italy.
Italy is the destination Aeneas pursues, although Dido says he does not know where its kingdoms are and may reach the desired land only as a stranger, perhaps in old age.

l: Dido and Aeneas's love affair, Heroides and Amores, VII
s: Dido recalls that the affair began when rain drove them into a cave, which she interprets as a sign of her doom. She continues to love Aeneas even while complaining of his faithlessness and feeling shame before Sychaeus.

l: Aeneas's departure from Carthage, Heroides and Amores, VII
s: Aeneas's departure is imminent, but storms temporarily obstruct his voyage. Dido asks him to delay until the sea and his cruelty have become calmer, offering herself, Carthage, and her resources as reasons to stay.

l: Dido's suicide, Heroides and Amores, VII
s: Dido presents her death as the consequence of Aeneas's departure and says that Aeneas will be regarded as its cause. She writes with a Trojan sword beside her, watches tears fall onto it, and tells Anna that she will soon give the final offerings to her ashes.

l: the sea, Heroides and Amores, VII
s: The sea is described as stormy, dangerous, and capable of punishing those who have broken faith. Dido fears that Aeneas may be shipwrecked and asks him to wait until the waters become calm.

l: faithlessness and broken promises, Heroides and Amores, VII
s: Dido accuses Aeneas of abandoning her, breaking his pledge, and repeating the deception he practiced before. She warns that the sea exacts punishment for faithlessness, especially when love has been wronged.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, 169 weii (]0 J know the seas that break upon
s: Dido writes to Aeneas, asking him to delay his departure because the sea, his weary comrades, and his damaged fleet require rest. She appeals to their past kindnesses, his possible debt to her, and her hope of wedlock, while asking for time to calm her love and endure her sorrow. If Aeneas refuses, she threatens to take her own life, describing the sword in her lap and the tears falling upon it. She asks her sister Anna to perform the final rites and declares that Aeneas provided both the cause of her death and the sword.

l: Aeneas, Heroides and Amores, 169 weii (]0 J know the seas that break upon
s: Aeneas is asked to delay his departure and allow the sea, his comrades, and his damaged fleet time to recover. Dido says that his refusal will cause her to take her own life and declares that he has provided both the cause of her death and the sword.

l: Dido, Heroides and Amores, 169 weii (]0 J know the seas that break upon
s: Dido (Elissa) writes to Aeneas, asking for a short delay so that her love and sorrow may grow calm and she may learn to endure. She threatens suicide if he refuses and says that she will be remembered as having fallen by her own hand.

l: the sea, Heroides and Amores, 169 weii (]0 J know the seas that break upon
s: The sea around the African shores has times when it grants and denies passage. Dido asks for time while the sea and her love grow calm.
